source_text:
Δοξάζω Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν τὸν θεὸν τὸν οὕτως ὑμᾶς σοφίσαντα: ἐνόησα γὰρ ὑμᾶς κατηρτισμένους ἐν ἀκινήτῳ πίστει, ὥσπερ καθηλωμένους ἐν τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ σαρκί τε καὶ πνεύματι καὶ ἡδρασμένους ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἐν τῷ αἵματι Χριστοῦ, πεπληροφορημένους εἰς τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν, ἀληθῶς ὄντα ἐκ γένους Δαυεὶδ κατὰ σάρκα, υἱὸν θεοῦ κατὰ θέλημα καὶ δύναμιν θεοῦ, γεγεννημένον ἀληθῶς ἐκ παρθένου, βεβαπτισμένον ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου, ἵνα πληρωθῇ πᾶσα δικαιοσύνη ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ:
ἀληθῶς ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου καὶ Ἡρώδου τετράρχου καθηλωμένον ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐν σαρκί, ἀφ̓ οὖ καρποῦ ἡμεῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ θεομακαρίστου αὐτοῦ πάθους, ἵνα ἄρῃ σύσσημον εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας διὰ τῆς ἀναστάσεως εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους καὶ πιστοὺς αὐτοῦ, εἴτε ἐν Ἰουδαίοις εἴτε ἐν ἔθνεσιν, ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι τῆς ἐκκλησίας αὐτοῦ.
thought_title: Christ's real flesh, Davidic descent, and cross
orientation: Ignatius opens his letter to the Smyrnaeans by praising God for their firm faith and rehearsing the true facts of Christ's incarnation, baptism, crucifixion, and resurrection.
pass_a_gloss: I glorify Jesus Christ the God who thus made you wise; for I perceived you [as] having been fitted together in unshakable faith, just as [if] nailed in the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ in flesh and in spirit, and [as] having been grounded in love in the blood of Christ, [as] having been fully assured concerning our Lord, [who is] truly being from the family of David according to flesh, son of God according to will and power of God, [who was] truly born from a virgin, [who was] baptized by John, in order that all righteousness might be fulfilled by him; [who was] truly under Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch nailed for us in flesh, from which fruit we [are] from his divinely blessed passion, in order that he might raise a banner for the ages through the resurrection for his holy and faithful ones, whether among Jews or among Gentiles, in one body of his church.

choices.why: The verb means to be knit or joined into a coherent whole, matching Ignatius's emphasis on unity.
The verb is specific to nailing, and Ignatius uses it to stress the physical reality of the cross.
The perfect participle conveys settled conviction about Christ's identity.
The noun denotes a military standard or signal raised for gathering; 'banner' preserves the image of a rallying sign.
The compound adjective intensifies 'blessed' with a divine source, and the glossary's literal lane requires keeping the compound sense.
The relative phrase points back to the cross as the source of the church's life; 'fruit' is the literal image Ignatius uses.

pass_b_english: I glorify Jesus Christ, the God who has made you so wise. For I have understood that you are fitted together in an unshakable faith, as if nailed to the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ in both flesh and spirit, and grounded in love by the blood of Christ. You are fully assured about our Lord, who is truly of the family of David according to the flesh, Son of God by the will and power of God, truly born of a virgin, baptized by John so that all righteousness might be fulfilled by him.

He was truly nailed in the flesh for us under Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch. We are the fruit of his divinely blessed passion, so that he might raise a sign for the ages through the resurrection for his holy and faithful ones, whether among Jews or among Gentiles, in one body of his church.

problems.why: Greek says 'from which fruit WE [are]'—meaning believers are the fruit of Christ's passion, not 'come from' it.

problems.quote: Of this fruit we are, from his divinely blessed passion
problems.why: Inverted syntax; 'Of this fruit we are' = 'We are of this fruit'.
problems.fix: Revise: 'We are the fruit of his divinely blessed passion.'

edits.old: Of this fruit we are, from his divinely blessed passion
edits.new: We are the fruit of his divinely blessed passion

problems.quote: raise a banner for the ages
problems.why: 'Banner' (sēmeion) usually means 'sign' or 'standard'; military metaphor may be unintended.
problems.fix: 'Raise a sign' or 'set up a standard' with note.

edits.old: raise a banner for the ages
edits.new: raise a sign for the ages

fixed: Changed 'raise a banner' to 'raise a sign' because σύσσημον (sēmeion) means 'sign' or 'standard,' not specifically 'banner'; the military metaphor is not clearly intended in the source.
